- At approximately **−20°C and below**, a short-trip or stop-start duty cycle can be much worse than a simple “30–40% range loss” rule of thumb, especially with cabin heat, payload, headwinds, snow/slush rolling resistance, and repeated cooling between stops.
- Battery heating itself consumes energy. A vehicle parked unplugged for extended periods may need material energy just to bring the pack into a suitable charging or high-power-discharge condition.
- In extreme heat, high pack temperature and high state of charge can cause **charge-power derating**, active cooling loads, and increased calendar aging. This is particularly relevant to vehicles with inadequate thermal management or demanding high-utilization service.
- For fleets, chargers and sites are part of the system: connector handling, icing, charger derating/faults, queueing, and depot electrical capacity can be as consequential as vehicle battery behavior.

But those facts do not establish that EVs generally *cannot* operate effectively in such climates. They establish that effective operation requires appropriate vehicle selection, thermal management, charging infrastructure, and winter/hot-weather operational planning.

The underlying measured evidence is not speculative. For instance, AAA’s controlled 2019 test measured roughly **41% range reduction at 20°F (−7°C) with cabin heat**, versus about **12% at the same temperature without cabin conditioning**; at **95°F (35°C)** with A/C, it measured about **17% reduction**. Those figures are not universal forecasts, but they confirm the direction and potentially large magnitude of the effect. Cold-climate real-world operation in Norway, Finland, Canada, and northern North America similarly demonstrates feasibility, while also demonstrating why winter range margins and charging strategy matter.

So the corrected, practice-oriented statement is:

> **EVs can be effective in extreme heat and cold, but not as drop-in, no-compromise replacements for an equivalent nominal-range vehicle in every use case. Extreme temperatures can impose large and operationally material penalties—especially for cold-soaked vehicles, high HVAC loads, fast charging, and demanding commercial duty cycles.**

If your experience concerns a particular application—such as heavy-duty trucking, emergency response, remote mining, buses with door-open cycles, or depot fleets—the operational conclusion may indeed be much less favorable than for privately owned passenger cars.
